 San Francisco residents clean up after deluge, shore up storm defenses 
 Downtown San Francisco set a new daily rainfall record for Nov. 18, breaking the old mark from 1918. 
 By Ginger Conejero Saab and Sergio Quintana • 
 Published November 19, 2026 • 
 Updated on November 19, 2026 at 5:17 pm 
 BOOKMARKER 
 NBC Universal, Inc. 
 Crews and residents in San Francisco spent time Thursday cleaning up after Wednesday’s record-breaking rainfall caused flooding across the city. Sergio Quintana reports. 
 Crews and residents in San Francisco spent time Thursday cleaning up after Wednesday's record-breaking rainfall caused flooding across the city.
 Public Works crews were spotted clearing and cleaning along Marina Boulevard after the street was overwhelmed with water Wednesday.

 Videos shared with NBC Bay Area showed drivers navigating high water and floodwaters flowing into people's homes.
 With well over 2 inches of rain on Wednesday, downtown San Francisco set a new daily rainfall record for Nov. 18 , breaking the old mark from 1918.

 During a news conference, the city's Public Utilities Commission acknowledged that its sewage and wastewater systems were overwhelmed.
 City leaders blamed the widespread flooding on the tremendous amount of rainfall in a short period of time, combined with high tides.
 "It can hold 200 million gallons of water at one time, but when you have this level of intensity, no system that we can reasonably design can meet that level of service," said Dennis Herrera with the Public Utilities Commission.
 Residents along Marina Boulevard said flooding is nothing new. One resident did express concern about waste being left behind after floodwaters receded.
 "When that actually recedes, you will see waste on the streets," the resident said. "There's waste up and down the street."
 Public Utilities Commission crews fanned out across the city Thursday to spray streets down, trying to clear away some of the sewage carried in by the floodwaters.
 In preparation for the next round of rain, residents raced to shore up their defenses. With a mad rush on sandbags, Public Works had to bring in a second full truckload, and that all happened before midday. Residents lined up, some waiting for nearly an hour, to pick up 10 bags per household.
 Residents said they barely averted some expensive losses and wanted to be extra prepared for any future flooding.
 "I almost lost $100,000 of Pokémon cards," Elmer Fulgencio said. "I have them all in my garage."
